v.why: Low learning rates leave the net undertrained in 243 epochs, so increasing it gives large gains.
At already high learning rates a further increase causes divergence and accuracy collapse.
Small batches already give noisy gradients, so a higher learning rate is more destabilizing.
With a low learning rate, fewer update steps from larger batches worsens undertraining.
With a high learning rate, larger batches reduce gradient noise and stabilize training.
Alpha near 1 over-regularizes, so increasing it further hurts accuracy.
Wider layers amplify the effective step size, making high learning rates less stable.
Deeper nets are more prone to instability under high learning rates.
With tiny steps, extra width speeds up fitting and adds capacity.
Going to very small batches adds noise and instability without much benefit.

raw:
These ten hypotheses come from reasoning about how Adam behaves over 243 epochs, not from any analysis of the benchmark data. I did not run anything against the tables.

1. Raising the learning rate helps more when the starting rate is low, because 1e-5 to 1e-4 is badly undertrained in 243 epochs.
2. Raising the learning rate hurts more when the starting rate is already high, because it pushes training toward divergence.
3. Raising the learning rate hurts more when the batch size is small, because small batches already give noisy gradients.
4. Raising the batch size hurts more when the learning rate is low, because fewer update steps compound the undertraining.
5. Raising the batch size helps more when the learning rate is high, because less gradient noise stabilizes training.
6. Raising alpha hurts more when alpha is already high, because values near 1 over-regularize.
7. Raising the width hurts more when the learning rate is high, because wider layers make large steps more unstable.
8. Raising the depth hurts more when the learning rate is high, because deeper nets are more prone to instability.
9. Raising the width helps more when the learning rate is low, because extra capacity speeds fitting when steps are tiny.
10. Lowering the batch size hurts more when the batch size is already small, because going from 6 to 4 adds noise without much benefit.
